alignment.note: Greek and Latin open with the connective καί / Et ('and'), a paratactic Markan opener. The Peshitta instead uses the postpositive particle ܕܝܢ (token 1, 'but/now'), which it places after the subject — a stylistic adjustment to Syriac discourse structure rather than a semantic change.

The Peshitta's postpositive ܕܝܢ ('but/now') corresponds functionally to the initial conjunction attested by the Greek καί and Latin Et; it is grouped here as the Syriac equivalent of that connective, displaced after the subject per Syriac syntax.

Greek and Latin preserve the Semitic-flavoured pleonastic participle ἀποκριθεὶς / respondens ('answering'), reflecting the Hebraic 'answered and said' idiom. The Peshitta omits this participle entirely, rendering only the finite verb of speaking — a frequent Syriac simplification of the doubled verb construction.
βλέπεις / ܚܙܐ ܐܢܬ / Vides — the Syriac uses the participle ܚܙܐ plus the explicit enclitic pronoun ܐܢܬ to express the second-person present, where Greek and Latin inflect a single finite verb.

The Vulgate inserts omnes ('all'), with no counterpart in either the Greek (ταύτας τὰς μεγάλας οἰκοδομάς) or the Syriac. This is a Latin amplification heightening the totality of the temple buildings; cf. the synoptic parallel Matt 24:1–2 where the disciples display 'all' the buildings.
οἰκοδομάς / ܒܢܝܢܐ / ædificationes; the Syriac places its noun before the adjective per normal Syriac word order, hence the index inversion relative to Greek.

Greek employs the emphatic double negation οὐ μή ('by no means') governing the aorist subjunctive; Latin renders this with a simple Non plus future indicative (relinquetur), and Syriac with ܠܐ plus a participle (ܡܫܬܒܩܐ). All three convey emphatic prophetic denial, but only the Greek preserves the strong subjunctive negation construction.

Greek ὧδε ('here') and its Syriac equivalent ܗܪܟܐ are both present, but the Vulgate omits any locative adverb, dropping the deictic 'here' from relinquetur lapis super lapidem. The Latin tradition thereby loses the emphasis on the immediate temple location.

Greek introduces the final clause with relative ὃς plus the double negative οὐ μή; Latin matches with relative qui non, while Syriac fuses the relative and negative into the single particle ܕܠܐ ('that not'). The Syriac construction is semantically equivalent but morphologically compresses the relative-plus-negation into one form.

Greek καταλυθῇ ('be thrown/torn down', from καταλύω) and Latin destruatur ('be destroyed') denote demolition. The Syriac ܡܣܬܬܪܐ derives from a root of overturning/dismantling and renders the same idea, though its semantic field of 'undoing' is slightly broader than the strict architectural 'throw down' of the Greek.
